en: Having thus instructed the procedure for the practice (*sādhanavidhi*) of the Blessed One, he leads [the practitioner] through the meditation on various deities by means of the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth, for the sake of pacification (*śāntika*) and other rites. "Listen," and so forth. *Vajra* refers to Vajragarbha, just as *Bhīma* refers to Bhīmasena. "The one to be accomplished" (*sādhyām*) refers to pacification, enrichment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśya*), protection (*rakṣā*), and malevolent rites (*abhicāra*). Specifically, according to the distinctions of caste (*varṇa*) and so forth: pacification is for present harm, while protection is for future harm.

"Of the wheel with nine compartments and so forth" means: that which has nine compartments consisting of eight spokes together with the central hub (*varaṭa*), and which is the "first" wheel in relation to the wheels to be described later. On its exterior is the rim (*nemi*). One should visualize the "caste, disposition for ritual action, and so forth"—that is, the caste and mental disposition corresponding to the ritual action—as belonging to "this," namely the seed-syllables (*bīja*) such as *tā* and others of the mantra. For all the compartments starting from the east and southeast, [the syllables are]: the *praṇava* is *oṃ*; *hutaṃ* is *svāhā*; its final letter is *hā*. "The name in the middle" means...

Between the syllables *varaṭe* and *oṃ hāḥ*, one should place the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) together with the words of protection. Equanimity-knowledge is emptiness-knowledge; one should make oneself endowed with that very emptiness. The omniscient equanimity, which is emptiness-knowledge, is the supreme protection when cultivated within the locus and the wheel (*cakra*). Therefore, one should apply it. This being so, protection arises for the wise. "Fear" means the occurrence of calamities; the meaning is that it does not exist even at a distance.

Then, by means of non-existence and emptiness, [the text mentions] "of sentient beings," which is an elliptical expression for the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). "The state of yoga" refers to the accomplishment of the deity. "In the eyes" means in the two eyes; "in the nose" means in the two nostrils. The syllables located within the cavities of the head and so forth—one should accomplish all rites, such as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and others. Regarding the reading "of all deities" found in some versions, the meaning is "even all deities."

This is the meaning: having contemplated the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*), one should instantly visualize a white lotus upon a moon disc, which has transformed from the syllable *TĀṂ*. Upon its center is a blue lotus marked by the syllable *TĀṂ*, which transforms into the Noble Tārā, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, adorned with various jewels and ornaments, her right hand granting fearlessness and her left holding a blue lotus. Having visualized oneself thus, sealed by Vairocana, and having armored oneself with the mantras as prescribed, one should place the syllable *OṂ* at the hub of an eight-spoked wheel situated on the moon within the heart-lotus, [reciting] "Devadatta."

One should contemplate: "Rakṣa hā! Tuttāre ture svāhā," proceeding from the eastern fire-pit and the others in a clockwise direction. Furthermore, the color of the Blessed Lady, as well as that of the lotus, the syllables of the wheel, and the rays, should be understood according to the ritual action (*karman*). In that regard, it is white for pacification (*śānti*) and protection (*rakṣā*); yellow for nourishment (*puṣṭi*); red for subjugation (*vaśya*); and black for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*). One should recite the mantra while visualizing the object of the rite (*sādhya*) being pervaded by the abundant rays of the syllables of the wheel within one's own body.

Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā. The interlacing [of mantras] should be performed with *svāhā* at the beginning as appropriate; however, during the time of preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), one should not interlace them.

Having written the syllables of the lotus, moon, and wheel upon birch bark, one should insert them along with the bark through the upper opening into the interior, unify them with the heart-lotus and other centers, and then extract them through the lower opening of the Blessed Lady’s lotus; if one retains [the object], it will become desired. This is the tradition regarding the consecration of the Vidyā. Furthermore, this procedure should be understood as applicable, as appropriate, to the two yogas that are about to be described. For the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*), Kurukullā is preeminent; she is the Blessed Lady Tārā herself.

Immediately following the meditation on emptiness, [one visualizes] Kurukullā, who arises instantaneously upon a sun disk resting on a red lotus and a corpse. She is transformed from a red syllable *Hrīḥ* and is seated upon a red utpala flower that has been transformed [from the same seed-syllable]. She is red in color, with one face, and three round, rolling red eyes; her tawny hair stands upright. She is sealed by Amitābha and is adorned with ornaments such as a wheel of five skulls upon her head. A garland of severed heads hangs from her neck. She has four arms: in her two right hands she holds a bud of a red utpala and an arrow, and in her two left hands she holds a hook made of red flowers and [the other implements].

For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should recite the mantra while visualizing oneself as [the goddess] holding a red flower-bow and a red lotus, dancing in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*). She draws in the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) by means of rays from the syllables of the wheel situated in the sun at her own heart; she causes that person to become overwhelmed, and binding him by the neck with a lotus, she presses a man against his heart and a woman against her womb with a hook, piercing them with a multitude of arrows—thus one should meditate upon oneself.

The wheel, which will be described, is six-cornered and situated upon an eight-petaled lotus and a sun disk. On the spokes one should join the syllables: *oṃ kurukulle svā*; in the center: *hrīḥ amukīṃ vaśīkuru hrīḥ hā*. The writing material will be described. The procedure for binding, pacifying, and so forth should be inferred according to the requirements. Regarding "ghorā" and so on: it is [the mantra] of the nāgas. This is auspicious for the pacification of fever, untimely death, and poison. Regarding "this is protection": taking it as "this" and "that protection. (269v/542) "By a hundred mantrins" refers to those possessing knowledge (*jñānin*), because of their compassion.

The Wisdom Wheel says: "Eight," and so forth. *Dala* means petal or spoke. First is the Tārā wheel. By the previously mentioned procedure for ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so on. Alternatively, having first contemplated emptiness and washed away the impurities of embodied beings, [one contemplates] that which is endowed with the characteristics of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth; this is connected to the phrase "the form of equanimity" (*samatārūpa*). By the method previously stated. Of this mantra that is about to be described. Through the state of being the object of meditation, again and again, with an extraordinary aspiration.

One should meditate on the self as "the nature of wisdom," that is, the self as the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). "Recited" means through recitation; "seed" refers to the mantra. The yoga for increasing wisdom is the yoga of the wheel of the Perfection of Wisdom.

This is the meaning: immediately after the meditation on emptiness, one should visualize oneself as Prajñāpāramitā—white in color, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, adorned with jewel ornaments and the like, marked by Akṣobhya, and possessing two arms. She holds a lotus with two stalks rising from between her left and right sides; these support a Prajñāpāramitā manuscript and a white lotus, which she grasps at the elbows with both hands while remaining in the *vyākhyāna* (teaching) mudrā. One should meditate upon oneself in this form.

"The placement of syllables on the wheel is like that of the Tārā mantra. To destroy the afflictions such as delusion and the rest, he teaches the yoga of Vairocana and the others, beginning with "On the moon," and so forth. The syllable is the syllable *vuṃ*. The wheel and bell are on the two right [hands].

This is the meaning: immediately after emptiness (*śūnyatā*), upon a moon disc within a red skull-cup filled with a universal lotus, one should meditate on oneself as Vairocana—white in color, wearing a crown of matted hair, performing the *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), and having arisen from the syllable *vūṃ* which is established upon a wheel-mark. He dispels the darkness of ignorance of the world by means of rays of light arising from the seed-syllable situated at his heart, together with the self-nature deities (*svābhadevatā*), and establishes all beings in Buddhahood. This procedure is to be applied accordingly in the subsequent sections as well; therefore, he says "by this," and so forth.

Its seed-syllable is ĀṂ; its emblem is a nine-faceted jewel. By means of jewels and so forth, there is the removal of pride regarding status and the like. In the two right hands are a jewel and a goad, which pacify passion. The seed-syllable of Amitābha is HRĪḤ; his emblem is a lotus. In the two left hands are a lotus and an arrow, which pacify hatred. The seed-syllable of Amoghasiddhi is KHAṂ; his emblem is a sword. In the two right hands are a sword and a goad, which pacify envy. The element of space (khadhātu) will be described below; here, "bhaga" refers to the sky, which is the source of phenomena (dharmodayā).

The intended meaning is that the Vajradhātu-maṇḍala, which will be described, resides within the *dharmodayā*. For this very reason, he will later refer to it as the "secret maṇḍala. By this, he indicates that the eight deities beginning with Vairocana are to be meditated upon in the maṇḍala, since they are mentioned here separately; thus, each one is to be visualized individually. As for the four goddesses beginning with Locanā, they should be understood as residing on lotuses and moon discs within the *dharmodayā* during their individual meditations. The symbol (*cihna*) of Locanā is a wheel.

In the right hands are the wheel, the vajra, the sword, and the arrow; on the crown are five skull-cups. The deities beginning with Vairocana also possess ornaments such as the wheel and so forth. [This practice] pacifies diseases and other calamities. Māmakī’s emblem is the vajra; in her right hands are the vajra, the wheel, the jewel, the lotus, the sword, and the arrow. She bestows grace upon those who are afraid and others. Pāṇḍarā’s emblem is the lotus; in her right hands are the lotus, the vajra, the sword, and the arrow. She brings nourishment to those who are emaciated. Tārā’s emblem is the red utpala lotus.
In the right hands are a red lotus, a sword, a goad, and an arrow; this is for the subjugation of enemies and others.
He summarizes: "Thus, by means of these various methods, while acting for the benefit of others, one becomes equal to Vajradhara at the ultimate limit of excellence."
The eighth mañjarī in the Sampuṭaṭīkā, [entitled] the Āmnāyamañjarī.
